sources.summary: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it. For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building. sources.summary: The Oscar-winner plays a Muslim contract killer in a boisterous, blackly comic thriller with shades of John Woo and Tarantino There are shades of John Woo and Tarantino here in a black-comic thriller from Pakistani-American director Bassam Tariq. There are shades also of Blade, the Marvel character that this film’s star, Mahershala Ali, had been preparing to play in a planned but then cancelled MCU movie which Tariq was going to direct. Here Ali plays Latif, a military veteran turned hitman for hire who uses knives and swords, not guns, and just happens to be a devout Muslim. The title refers to the Islamic tradition in which Muhammad was asked three times who is the most deserving of respect and replied each time: “Your mother.” It is, however, this film’s semi-intentional irony that mothers and female authority figures are largely irrelevant in it, the drama being more about men without women. Latif is just finishing off a chaotic wet job in a squalid public bathroom one day, when he takes a call on his mobile from his teenage daughter Fatiha (played by Adia, from Steven Soderbergh’s streaming series Full Circle) telling him that his wife, Fatiha’s mother, has died. Convulsed with guilt at having neglected the family home for his homicidal profession, Latif arrives back to find his son Qadir (Jahleel Kamara) acting out, and his newborn baby allergic to formula, and only able to drink the expressed breast milk of which his late wife has left a limited stockpile in the fridge. So now this tough guy has to put the baby in a papoose and go around getting breast milk from Muslim family charities. Continue reading...

sources.summary: In her new film, the actor plays a lawyer taking on the French state over reproductive rights. She talks about being criticised for her support of Israel and pushed to the limit by Lars von Trier While she was making the film Women on Trial , about the real-life trial of a child prosecuted for having an abortion, someone sent Charlotte Gainsbourg a photograph of her mother at one of the pro-choice demonstrations that erupted in France at the time. It was “very moving”, says Gainsbourg to see her mother, the actor Jane Birkin, in 1972, “looking beautiful and in the middle of a demonstration”. At that time, in a court in Bobigny, a Paris suburb, the prominent lawyer Gisèle Halimi was defending 16-year-old Marie-Claire Chevalier, as well as her mother and two other women who helped her have an abortion, then illegal in France. The Bobigny trial was new to her, says Gainsbourg, who plays Halimi, a leading figure in French feminism and activism who died in 2020. “I had no idea. For me, abortion rights started with Simone Veil” – the French minister of health who saw through decriminalisation three years later – “so I had to catch up.” Continue reading...
